articles.title: Ukraine cannot be settled like a business deal
articles.body:
Ukraine cannot be settled like a business deal
Diplomatic efforts to end an acute and bloody armed conflict should always be welcomed and the persistence of Donald Trump’s administration, which has pursued this goal for more than a year and a half, also deserves recognition, even if the results so far can hardly be called outstanding.
At the very least, the White House remains the only actor in the West both attempting to change the situation and possessing significant leverage over it. Trump and his closest associates probably do genuinely want the war to end as its continuation distracts Washington from foreign policy priorities they regard as more important. But why, then, does Trump’s diplomatic initiative keep going round in circles, with each new attempt ending in another disappointment?
Trump and his principal envoys tend to approach the conflict as an extraordinarily difficult but essentially technical problem, as a puzzle to be solved in isolation from the wider international system. This reflects the worldview of the current White House, where international affairs are a collection of practical problems to be resolved in ways that strengthen America’s position, preferably with some commercial benefit attached. Given the professional backgrounds of the president and his two principal intermediaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, this is hardly surprising.
Such an approach can be useful as an instrument, but it becomes less useful when it substitutes for an understanding of the processes that produced the conflict in the first place and, to use the Russian formulation, its root causes. Any durable settlement requires some understanding of what must change in relations between the major powers if similar confrontations are to be avoided.
Trump repeatedly insists that the war would never have begun had he been president in 2022 with the implication that Joe Biden and the Democrats were simply too incompetent to prevent it. Trump has occasionally acknowledged that NATO’s long expansion eastward contributed to the crisis, but he generally shows little interest in the broader military and political processes behind it.
Yet American and NATO policy towards Ukraine wasn’t created by one administration or a handful of officials in Washington and Brussels, rather it developed over decades from a particular conception of Western strategic interests. The crisis that entered its most acute phase in 2022 was, from Moscow’s perspective, the culmination of processes underway since the end of the Cold War.
This helps explain why Washington continues to underestimate how much the outcome matters to the principal participants. For both Russia and Ukraine, too much is at stake for the conflict to be settled through the kind of transaction Trump instinctively favors, given their interests are obviously opposed, but both regard the outcome as fateful. Western Europe, having invested heavily in Ukraine’s cause, also has a direct political stake in the result, so every new attempt by Washington’s two brokers therefore encounters the same obstacle in that none of the parties sees this as simply another deal.
There’s another contradiction in the American position because Washington wishes to become the principal mediator in a conflict whose continuation it has materially supported.The US position has certainly changed under Trump as Washington’s previous fixation on Ukraine has diminished considerably. Trump would prefer America to step back while retaining decisive influence over what happens next, but that is precisely where the difficulty begins.
Transferring the financial burden, political responsibility and risks to the Western Europeans while continuing to dictate the terms requires a degree of obedience from junior partners that Washington can no longer guarantee. EU governments and Kiev have also learnt how to deal with this unconventional president and when they can’t persuade him, they have become increasingly adept at circumventing his pressure.
The one American instrument against which there would be little defence is a complete cessation of military support, but Trump is unlikely to take that step, even if he were personally inclined to do so because facilitating an outright Russian victory isn’t his objective. He may care less than his predecessor about the precise shape of the eventual settlement, but a complete Ukrainian defeat would be another matter. Nor would abandoning Ukraine enjoy much support across the American political establishment, where there is virtually no constituency for a fundamental rapprochement with Russia.
The White House therefore doesn’t envisage the radical change in American policy that would be necessary to transform the conflict, but without one, events tend to return to their previous course as a prolonged and extremely fierce confrontation whose duration nobody can confidently predict.
In such a confrontation, those fighting the war and bearing its risks ultimately matter more than mediators or outside sponsors. None of this means Witkoff and Kushner’s shuttle diplomacy is pointless, given communication between adversaries is indispensable, and the present infrastructure for official dialogue remains inadequate. Also, informal channels can help restore understanding where formal diplomacy has broken down, but informal diplomacy has limits.
Friends and business associates may establish contacts and discover areas in which compromise is conceivable, but they don’t themselves make peace. The shuttle diplomacy of a presidential son-in-law and a trusted business partner may eventually serve as a catalyst for serious negotiations, however, if that moment comes, the settlement will have to be negotiated by officials and institutions possessing state legitimacy and the power to implement what they sign. Personal connections can open the door, but they can’t, by themselves, end a war.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by RT.

articles.title: How are NATO DIANA innovators improving wound care on the front lines?
articles.body:
Combat wound care and management have come a long way over the last few decades. And while advances in trauma care have helped save countless lives on the battlefield, preventing infection and supporting recovery after the initial injury can be just as important.
In operational environments where evacuation may not be possible and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an increasing concern, there is a growing need for technologies that improve the way we treat wounds in the battlefield.
Innovators in NATO DIANA’s 2026 cohort are helping to meet that need by developing new approaches to wound care. From light-activated antimicrobial therapies to phage-based precision therapeutics and treatments, innovative solutions could revolutionise wound care for both civilian trauma patients and military personnel.
GutSee – Decoding the microbiome to treat infections
GutSee Health is a UK biotechnology company pioneering precision therapies for bacterial diseases. Its proprietary AI platform uses microbiome data to create precision treatments based on bacteriophage therapy. Phages are naturally occurring viruses that seek out and destroy specific bacteria without harming beneficial ones. This makes them useful for treating a variety of problems, from infected battlefield injuries to ongoing gut conditions like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Although the science behind phage therapy is well established, developing these treatments remains fragmented, manual and focused on individual patients.
GutSee’s platform brings four key stages into one integrated process. First, it matches bacterial strains with the phages most likely to destroy them. Second, it predicts how bacteria may evolve and mutate, helping treatments stay ahead of emerging resistance. Third, it designs mixtures of several phages combined with beneficial bacteria to improve the overall bacterial balance rather than simply remove a harmful pathogen. Finally, it connects treatment design with manufacturing and clinical use. Together, these stages form a continuous learning cycle that improves treatment recommendations, accelerating therapy development by up to 98% compared with traditional laboratory-heavy processes.
GutSee is initially focusing on combat and civilian wound infections, working with NATO, governments and foundations, with support from the Ukrainian government. Longer term, GutSee plans to license its platform for further areas, including gut disorders and oncology.
LightOx – Using light to help control wound infections
LightOx is developing light-activated treatments that help kill harmful bacteria that colonise wounds. They produce a simple gel that can be applied directly to a wound. The gel is activated by a light, and the treatment helps kill harmful bacteria in a targeted way, right where the infection is developing.
In battlefield injuries, bacteria can quickly enter damaged tissue and cause infections that slow healing and increase the risk of complications, including sepsis, amputation, or even death. This is especially challenging when common antibiotics stop working against drug-resistant bacteria. LightOx’s approach offers a tool to help control infection in wounds while injured personnel await further treatment, while also fighting AMR.
Earlier this year, LightOx was recognised for its light-activated treatment for infected wounds, with an Outstanding Achievement Award at the Medilink Healthcare Business Awards 2026.
Deep Breathe – Helping medics detect hidden chest injuries faster
In battlefield trauma, injuries to the lungs or chest can be difficult to spot without hospital equipment, but failing to detect them can delay critical care. Deep Breathe, based in Canada, have developed a solution involving a portable ultrasound that frontline medical teams can use to detect serious chest and torso injuries faster, as well internal abdominal bleeding.
Deep Breathe combine ultrasound with AI that recognise signs of injuries such as a collapsed lung, bleeding in the chest, or bruising of lung tissue. Designed to work on phones or tablets and in places with limited or no connectivity, the technology could help medics make faster, more informed decisions closer to the point of injury, improving triage in remote areas and difficult environments.
By bringing this kind of support closer to the battlefield – at the point-of-injury – Deep Breathe’s solution could help improve diagnosis and treatment, avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures, and speeding up life-saving decisions when every second matters.
Biocellis – Instant detection of biological and chemical agents
After a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) attack, effective treatment requires a quick response and knowledge of the intoxicating agent. Biocellis is a company from France that has developed an ultra-sensitive diagnostic testing system that can rapidly detect and identify biological and chemical agents.
Traditionally, rapid testing methods sacrifice sensitivity and most sensitive tests do not provide results fast enough. Biocellis has patented a bioluminescence immunoassays platform that delivers laboratory grade sensitivity in less than 60 seconds. The technology uses a compact, portable format that is ideal for point-of-care and high-throughput screening.
Rapid and reliable detection helps clinicians treat patients with the most effective remedies available. Biocellis helps medical professionals understand what they are up against so that they can quickly provide the treatment and care that patients need.
These technologies are already filling some of the most urgent gaps in battlefield medicine. By giving frontline medical teams better tools to save lives and improve care when conditions are at their most challenging.
Through NATO DIANA, these innovators gain access to the tools and resources they need to take their promising, cutting-edge technologies from concept to real-world use. Through expertise from technical and defence mentors, opportunities to test their technologies, and access to operational exercises like Vigorous Warrior, innovators are supported by DIANA to ensure their solutions are not only technically strong, but deployable and relevant in the demanding environments where they are needed most.
Source: diana.nato.int

articles.title: US envoys pitch 30-km buffer zone to Putin in 3-hour meeting
articles.body:
Donald Trump's representatives meet Russian officials in Moscow to discuss a potential free trade zone and frozen asset transfers before heading to Kyiv.
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin for over three hours at the Kremlin Senate Palace on Sept. 5.
 The American representatives presented a proposal to end the war in Ukraine.
 The new offer includes establishing a 30-kilometer buffer zone in the Donbas region, sources close to the talks said.
 The proposal requires Russian and Ukrainian forces to withdraw from the frontline.
 The evacuated area would become a free trade zone, the sources said.
 It remains unclear which side will provide security in the proposed buffer zone.
 The envoys also discussed a new formula for frozen Russian assets.
 U.S. and European experts proposed transferring approximately 210 billion euros of frozen Russian assets from Belgium-based Euroclear to a new custodian structure controlled by the European Union.
 The U.S. delegation landed at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport earlier in the day.
 Putin's special envoy Kirill Dmitriyev welcomed the American representatives.
 Dmitriyev shared a message on social media calling the envoys messengers of peace.
 The U.S. motorcade initially headed to the American Embassy before arriving at the Kremlin for the 8 p.m. meeting.
 Putin expressed his readiness to discuss all options for resolving the conflict in Ukraine.
 He asked the envoys to convey his gratitude and best wishes to Trump before the talks began.
 The U.S. representatives are scheduled to arrive in Kyiv on Sept. 6 following a train journey from Poland.
 The envoys abandoned plans for a direct flight to the Ukrainian capital after Russian missiles struck the Zhuliany airport.
 Ukrainian officials express concern Putin might convince the U.S. representatives using his own arguments.
 Kyiv officials argue the American delegation should have started their diplomatic tour in the attacked country to maintain a balanced approach.

articles.title: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majority
articles.body:
The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has emerged as the winner in a crucial state election in Germany, exit polls have projected, securing a historic result and more than doubling its support. The AfD now appear on the brink of becoming the first far-right party to gain power in Germany at state level since the second world war.
Initial exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.4% of the vote, a larger share than predicted, and decisively larger than that of the Christian Democrats (CDU) of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world. However, it still remains unclear as to how and whether the AfD will be able to form a government, having ruled out entering a coalition and being refused any form of cooperation by the mainstream parties.
The CDU was trailing massively on around 18.4% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.3%, with the Social Democrats on 8.4% and the Greens on 8.7% by around early evening. The smaller BSW reached the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament, against expectations. The party, an offshoot of Die Linke, has agreed to cooperate with the AfD on issues such as energy price reform.
Participation was at a record high of 76.5%.
Votes are still being counted, but it appeared initially that the AfD might have failed to secure an absolute majority – the condition it has said is central to it taking power, given its refusal to govern with another party.
The CDU and all other mainstream parties have also refused to collude with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer, or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
Addressing jubilant supporters, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said: “We have made history in this country”. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD, he said his party was ready to reach out to all powers that strove for political change.
“We extend a hand to all democratic forces that wish to pursue better policies,” a beaming Siegmund said after exit polls had been published. He said themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate.
The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with the AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out.
Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era.
She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Siegmund on Sunday evening called Merz “a very good campaigner for the AfD”.
Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how the AfD could rule.
About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents.
Final polls had shown the AfD to have around 40-41% of support, and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%.
The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.
The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.
The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter.
In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.
If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms.
He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.
Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.
Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.
Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.
On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”
The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.
The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.
Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

articles.title: Russian Strike Hits Dnipro Logistics Warehouses, Injuring 2
articles.body:
Russian forces launched an attack on the city of Dnipro on Sunday, Sept. 6, striking warehouses operated by a logistics company and injuring at least two people, Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Head Oleksandr Hanzha reported.
The strike ignited a large fire at the commercial storage facilities, according to Hanzha’s statement on Telegram.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The enemy attacked Dnipro. As a result of the strike, a fire broke out at the warehouses of a logistics company,” Hanzha initially stated.
In a subsequent update, Hanzha confirmed that two civilians sustained injuries in the attack and were receiving necessary medical treatment, while emergency services worked to contain and extinguish the blaze.
Evening drone strikes kill five across four regions
The daytime attack on Dnipro follows a wave of Russian drone strikes late Saturday, Sept. 5, that killed at least five civilians and injured 17 others across the Kharkiv, Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Khmelnytskyi regions.
In the Kharkiv region, a Russian jet-powered drone hit a private residential area in central Chuhuiv, killing three members of a single family: a 45-year-old man, a 19-year-old woman, and an 11-year-old boy. The strike destroyed a private home, an outbuilding, and a garage, while severely injuring a woman and leaving three other residents suffering from acute stress reactions.
In the Kyiv region, Russian drones targeted the village of Lisne in the Bucha district, setting two private houses on fire. The attack killed two people, injured one, and damaged five homes alongside three vehicles.

In Zaporizhzhia, multiple drone strikes damaged residential houses and an administrative building late Saturday, injuring at least six people, including an elderly woman, while sparking several structure fires.
In Khmelnytskyi, a Russian drone struck a multi-story apartment block, injuring seven residents and destroying stairwells and structural floor slabs. Concurrent drone strikes also damaged commercial enterprises in the Khmelnytskyi district, triggering fires that were later brought under control by rescue crews.
